items.stem: In the α-particle scattering experiment, most α-particles passed straight through the gold foil. This showed that …
options: most of the atom is empty space
items.answer: most of the atom is empty space
items.markingKey: Very few α-particles came close to a nucleus.

items.stem: Describe the observations of the α-particle scattering experiment and state the conclusion drawn from each.
items.answer: Most passed straight through: atom mostly empty space. Some deflected through small angles: a positive charge concentrated in the atom. A very few deflected through > 90°: a tiny, dense, positive nucleus containing most of the mass.
items.markingKey: most undeflected → empty space [1]; small deflections → positive charge [1]; large deflections → small massive nucleus [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why an α-particle approaching a nucleus head-on is deflected back along its path.
items.answer: The α-particle and nucleus are both positive; the electrostatic repulsion increases as it approaches, doing work against its kinetic energy until it stops and is pushed back.
items.markingKey: electrostatic repulsion [1]; KE converted, stops and returns [1] [2]

items.stem: An atom of iron has a diameter of about 2.5 × 10⁻¹⁰ m and its nucleus has a diameter of about 9.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. Determine the ratio of atomic diameter to nuclear diameter.
items.markingKey: 2.5 × 10⁻¹⁰/9.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ = 2.6 × 10⁴. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: An atom of iron has a diameter of about 2.5 × 10⁻¹⁰ m and its nucleus about 9.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. In a scale model the nucleus is a marble 2.0 cm across. Calculate the diameter of the model atom in metres and use it to explain why most α-particles pass straight through a thin foil.
items.answer: 521 m; the nucleus occupies a tiny fraction of the atom so most α-particles do not pass near one.
items.markingKey: ratio = 2.6 × 10⁴ [1]; model diameter = 521 m [1]; mostly empty space explanation [1] [3]

items.stem: The α-particle scattering experiment provided evidence for the nuclear model of the atom. (a) Explain why the experiment is carried out in a vacuum. (b) Explain why the foil must be very thin. (c) Describe the structure of the atom suggested by these results.
items.answer: (a) α-particles would be absorbed/scattered by air molecules. (b) So each α-particle is scattered by only one nucleus. (c) Small, dense, positive nucleus with electrons around it; mostly empty space.
items.markingKey: (a) α-particles would be absorbed/scattered by air molecules [1] (b) So each α-particle is scattered by only one nucleus [1] (c) nucleus [1]; electrons/empty space [1] [2]

items.stem: A very small fraction of α-particles were deflected through more than 90°. This showed that …
options: the positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus
items.answer: the positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus
items.markingKey: Large deflections need a small, massive, positive centre.

items.stem: Explain why α-particle scattering is not affected significantly by the electrons in the gold atoms.
items.answer: Electrons have a very small mass compared with an α-particle (and small charge), so they cannot deflect it significantly.
items.markingKey: electron mass very small [1]; little deflection [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe the nuclear model of the atom.
items.answer: A tiny, positively charged nucleus containing protons and neutrons (most of the mass) surrounded by negatively charged electrons at relatively large distances; mostly empty space.
items.markingKey: small positive nucleus with most mass [1]; electrons outside, mostly empty space [1] [2]

items.stem: An α-particle in a scattering experiment passes far from any nucleus. Describe and explain its path. Suggest how the path would differ for a lower-energy α-particle on the same initial line.
items.answer: It travels straight through with negligible deflection because the repulsive force is negligible at large distances. A lower-energy α-particle would be deflected more.
items.markingKey: path described [1]; explained by electrostatic repulsion [1]; effect of energy [1] [3]

items.stem: An atom of carbon has a diameter of about 1.4 × 10⁻¹⁰ m and its nucleus has a diameter of about 5.4 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. What is the ratio of atomic diameter to nuclear diameter?
An atom of hydrogen has a diameter of about 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m and its nucleus has a diameter of about 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. Work out the ratio of atomic diameter to nuclear diameter.
items.markingKey: 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰/1.7 × 10⁻¹⁵ = 6.5 × 10⁴. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: An atom of hydrogen has a diameter of about 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m and its nucleus has a diameter of about 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. Determine the ratio of atomic diameter to nuclear diameter.
items.markingKey: 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰/1.7 × 10⁻¹⁵ = 6.5 × 10⁴. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: An atom of carbon has a diameter of about 1.4 × 10⁻¹⁰ m and its nucleus about 5.4 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. In a scale model the nucleus is a marble 2.0 cm across. Calculate the diameter of the model atom in metres and use it to explain why most α-particles pass straight through a thin foil.
items.answer: 519 m; the nucleus occupies a tiny fraction of the atom so most α-particles do not pass near one.
items.markingKey: ratio = 2.6 × 10⁴ [1]; model diameter = 519 m [1]; mostly empty space explanation [1] [3]

items.stem: In 1909 Geiger and Marsden fired α-particles at a thin gold foil in a vacuum and counted scattered particles at different angles. A student in Madrid is studying their results. (a) State the observation that shows that the nucleus contains most of the mass and is very small. (b) Explain why the foil must be very thin. (c) Sketch the paths of three α-particles passing at different distances from a nucleus.
items.answer: (a) A very small number were deflected through angles greater than 90°. (b) So each α-particle is scattered by only one nucleus. (c) distant: almost straight; nearer: small deflection; head-on: reflected back
items.markingKey: (a) A very small number were deflected through angles greater than 90° [1] (b) So each α-particle is scattered by only one nucleus [1] (c) distant path almost undeviated [1]; closer paths deflected more, head-on reflected back [1] [2]

items.stem: The α-particle scattering experiment provided evidence for the nuclear model of the atom. (a) State the observation that shows the atom is mostly empty space. (b) Sketch the paths of three α-particles passing at different distances from a nucleus. (c) Describe the structure of the atom suggested by these results.
items.answer: (a) Most α-particles passed straight through undeflected. (b) distant: almost straight; nearer: small deflection; head-on: reflected back (c) Small, dense, positive nucleus with electrons around it; mostly empty space.
items.markingKey: (a) Most α-particles passed straight through undeflected [1] (b) distant path almost undeviated [1]; closer paths deflected more, head-on reflected back [1] [2] (c) nucleus [1]; electrons/empty space [1] [2]

items.stem: A nucleus of ²³⁵₉₂U contains …
items.answer: 92 protons and 143 neutrons
items.markingKey: Neutrons = 235 − 92.

items.stem: Explain why the β-particles from a radioactive source have a continuous range of energies, while α-particles from one nuclide have a single energy.
items.answer: In β decay the energy released is shared between the β-particle and a (anti)neutrino in varying proportions; in α decay only two bodies share the energy, so each α has the same energy.
items.markingKey: energy shared with (anti)neutrino [1]; two-body α decay gives fixed energy [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties.
items.answer: They have the same number of protons and so the same number of electrons in the neutral atom; chemical behaviour depends on the electrons.
items.markingKey: same number of electrons [1]; chemistry depends on electrons [1] [2]

items.stem: A nucleus of ²³⁸₉₂U (nucleon number 238, proton number 92) undergoes α-decay. What are the nucleon number and proton number of the daughter nucleus?
items.answer: nucleon number 234, proton number 90
items.markingKey: ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + ⁴₂α; nucleon and proton numbers balance.

items.stem: A nucleus of ¹³₇N (nucleon number 13, proton number 7) undergoes β⁺ decay. Write the nuclear equation, showing nucleon and proton numbers, and state the particles emitted.
items.answer: ¹³₇N → ¹³₆C + ⁰₊₁e + νₑ
items.markingKey: daughter nuclide correct [1]; emitted particle(s) with nucleon and proton numbers [1]; (anti)neutrino included [1] [3]

items.stem: A nucleus of ⁴⁰₁₉K is a β⁺ emitter used in a research laboratory. (a) Write the decay equation. (b) State the antiparticle of the positron and how it differs.
items.answer: (a) ⁴⁰₁₉K → ⁴⁰₁₈Ar + ⁰₊₁e + νₑ (b) The electron: same mass, opposite charge.
items.markingKey: (a) daughter [1]; positron and neutrino [1] [2] (b) electron [1]; same mass opposite charge [1] [2]

items.stem: Isotopes of an element have …
options: the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
different numbers of electrons in the neutral atom
the same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons
items.answer: the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
items.markingKey: Same proton number, different nucleon number.

items.stem: Compare the charge, mass and penetrating power of α, β⁻ and γ radiation.
items.answer: α: +2e, 4u, stopped by paper; β⁻: −e, ~1/2000 u, stopped by a few mm of aluminium; γ: no charge or mass, reduced by thick lead.
items.markingKey: charges [1]; masses [1]; penetration [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why γ-emission does not change the nucleon number or proton number of a nucleus.
items.answer: A γ-ray photon has no charge and no mass; it carries away only energy from an excited nucleus.
items.markingKey: no charge and no mass [1]; only energy lost [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why γ-emission does not change the nucleon number or proton number of a nucleus. (b) Compare the charge, mass and penetrating power of α, β⁻ and γ radiation.
items.answer: (a) A γ-ray photon has no charge and no mass; it carries away only energy from an excited nucleus. (b) α: +2e, 4u, stopped by paper; β⁻: −e, ~1/2000 u, stopped by a few mm of aluminium; γ: no charge or mass, reduced by thick lead.
items.markingKey: (a) no charge and no mass [1]; only energy lost [1] [2] (b) charges [1]; masses [1]; penetration [1] [3]

items.stem: A nucleus of ⁴⁰₁₉K (nucleon number 40, proton number 19) undergoes β⁺ decay. What are the nucleon number and proton number of the daughter nucleus?
items.answer: nucleon number 40, proton number 18
items.markingKey: ⁴⁰₁₉K → ⁴⁰₁₈Ar + ⁰₊₁e + νₑ; nucleon and proton numbers balance.

items.stem: A nucleus of ²⁴¹₉₅Am (nucleon number 241, proton number 95) undergoes α-decay. What are the nucleon number and proton number of the daughter nucleus?
items.answer: nucleon number 237, proton number 93
items.markingKey: ²⁴¹₉₅Am → ²³⁷₉₃Np + ⁴₂α; nucleon and proton numbers balance.

items.stem: A nucleus of ⁶⁰₂₇Co (nucleon number 60, proton number 27) undergoes β⁻ decay. What are the nucleon number and proton number of the daughter nucleus?
items.answer: nucleon number 60, proton number 28
items.markingKey: ⁶⁰₂₇Co → ⁶⁰₂₈Ni + ⁰₋₁e + ν̄ₑ; nucleon and proton numbers balance.

items.stem: A nucleus of ²²⁶₈₈Ra decays by a series of 2 α-decays and 1 β⁻ decay. Determine the nucleon number and proton number of the final nucleus, and its number of neutrons.
items.answer: A = 218, Z = 85 (At); 133 neutrons

items.stem: The isotope ¹⁵₈O is used in medical imaging at a hospital in Dubai. It decays by β⁺ emission. (a) State the numbers of protons and neutrons in the nucleus. (b) Write the decay equation. (c) Explain why the positrons emitted have a range of kinetic energies.
items.answer: (a) 8 protons, 7 neutrons (b) ¹⁵₈O → ¹⁵₇N + ⁰₊₁e + νₑ (c) The energy released is shared with the neutrino in varying proportions.
items.markingKey: (a) both: 8 protons, 7 neutrons [1] (b) daughter [1]; positron and neutrino [1] [2] (c) The energy released is shared with the neutrino in varying proportions [1]

items.stem: A nucleus of ¹¹₆C is a β⁺ emitter used in a research laboratory. (a) State the numbers of protons and neutrons in the nucleus. (b) Write the decay equation. (c) State the antiparticle of the positron and how it differs.
items.answer: (a) 6 protons, 5 neutrons (b) ¹¹₆C → ¹¹₅B + ⁰₊₁e + νₑ (c) The electron: same mass, opposite charge.
items.markingKey: (a) both: 6 protons, 5 neutrons [1] (b) daughter [1]; positron and neutrino [1] [2] (c) electron [1]; same mass opposite charge [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the quark composition of a proton?
items.answer: uud
items.markingKey: Charge: +⅔ + ⅔ − ⅓ = +1.

items.stem: Explain why a proton is not a fundamental particle but an electron is.
items.answer: A proton is made of three quarks (uud), so it has internal structure; an electron (a lepton) is not made of smaller particles.
items.markingKey: proton made of quarks [1]; electron is fundamental lepton [1] [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between hadrons and leptons.
items.answer: Hadrons are made of quarks and experience the strong force (baryons and mesons); leptons are fundamental and do not experience the strong force (e.g. electron, neutrino).
items.markingKey: hadrons: quarks, strong force [1]; leptons: fundamental, no strong force [1] [2]

items.stem: The K⁺ meson has quark composition us̄. State the quark composition and the charge of its antiparticle, and explain how the masses compare.
items.answer: ūs; charge −e; same mass as the K⁺ meson
items.markingKey: each quark replaced by its antiquark (and vice versa): ūs [1]; charge −e [1]; same mass [1] [3]

items.stem: The Σ⁺ baryon has quark composition uus. State the quark composition and the charge of its antiparticle, and explain how the masses compare.
items.answer: ūūs̄; charge −e; same mass as the Σ⁺ baryon
items.markingKey: each quark replaced by its antiquark (and vice versa): ūūs̄ [1]; charge −e [1]; same mass [1] [3]

items.stem: Particle accelerators produce many hadrons, which can be described by the quark model. (a) State the charges of the up, down and strange quarks. (b) The π⁻ meson has quark composition ūd. Determine its charge. (c) State what is meant by an antiparticle.
items.answer: (a) u: +⅔e; d: −⅓e; s: −⅓e (b) −⅔ − ⅓ = −e (c) A particle with the same mass but opposite charge (and other quantum numbers).
items.markingKey: (a) u = +⅔e [1]; d and s = −⅓e [1] [2] (b) −⅔ − ⅓ = −e [1] (c) A particle with the same mass but opposite charge (and other quantum numbers) [1]

items.stem: What is the quark composition of a neutron?
items.answer: udd
items.markingKey: Charge: +⅔ − ⅓ − ⅓ = 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between a baryon and a meson.
items.answer: A baryon is made of three quarks (e.g. proton uud); a meson is made of a quark and an antiquark (e.g. π⁺ = ud̄).
items.markingKey: baryon three quarks with example [1]; meson quark-antiquark with example [1] [2]

items.stem: State the four fundamental interactions and the particles on which the strong interaction acts.
items.answer: Gravitational, electromagnetic, weak and strong; the strong force acts between hadrons (quarks) only.
items.markingKey: four forces [1]; strong acts on hadrons/quarks only [1] [2]

items.stem: Classify the neutron as a hadron or a lepton and justify your answer by describing its structure. State whether it experiences the strong interaction.
items.answer: Hadron (baryon): made of three quarks udd; feels the strong force.
items.markingKey: correct class [1]; structure [1]; strong force statement [1] [3]

items.stem: The K⁰ meson has quark composition ds̄. State the quark composition and the charge of its antiparticle, and explain how the masses compare.
items.answer: d̄s; charge 0; same mass as the K⁰ meson
items.markingKey: each quark replaced by its antiquark (and vice versa): d̄s [1]; charge 0 [1]; same mass [1] [3]

items.stem: The π⁻ meson has quark composition ūd. State the quark composition and the charge of its antiparticle, and explain how the masses compare.
items.answer: ud̄; charge +e; same mass as the π⁻ meson
items.markingKey: each quark replaced by its antiquark (and vice versa): ud̄ [1]; charge +e [1]; same mass [1] [3]

items.stem: The neutron has quark composition udd. State the quark composition and the charge of its antiparticle, and explain how the masses compare.
items.answer: ūd̄d̄; charge 0; same mass as the neutron
items.markingKey: each quark replaced by its antiquark (and vice versa): ūd̄d̄ [1]; charge 0 [1]; same mass [1] [3]

items.stem: The proton has quark composition uud. State the quark composition and the charge of its antiparticle, and explain how the masses compare.
items.answer: ūūd̄; charge −e; same mass as the proton
items.markingKey: each quark replaced by its antiquark (and vice versa): ūūd̄ [1]; charge −e [1]; same mass [1] [3]

items.stem: A student at a summer school in Mexico City is learning about the standard model of particle physics. (a) State the charges of the up, down and strange quarks. (b) Name two leptons. (c) Distinguish between hadrons and leptons in terms of the forces they experience.
items.answer: (a) u: +⅔e; d: −⅓e; s: −⅓e (b) electron and electron neutrino (also muon, tau, their neutrinos) (c) Hadrons feel the strong force; leptons do not.
items.markingKey: (a) u = +⅔e [1]; d and s = −⅓e [1] [2] (b) electron and electron neutrino (also muon, tau, their neutrinos) [1] (c) Hadrons feel the strong force; leptons do not [1]

items.stem: A student at a summer school in Lima is learning about the standard model of particle physics. (a) Use the quark model to show that the neutron is neutral. (b) The π⁻ meson has quark composition ūd. Determine its charge. (c) State what is meant by an antiparticle. (d) Name two leptons. (e) Distinguish between hadrons and leptons in terms of the forces they experience.
items.answer: (a) +⅔ − ⅓ − ⅓ = 0 (b) −⅔ − ⅓ = −e (c) A particle with the same mass but opposite charge (and other quantum numbers). (d) electron and electron neutrino (also muon, tau, their neutrinos) (e) Hadrons feel the strong force; leptons do not.

items.stem: In β⁻ decay, which quark change occurs?
options: An up quark changes into a down quark
A down quark changes into a strange quark
An up quark changes into a strange quark
A down quark changes into an up quark
items.answer: A down quark changes into an up quark
items.markingKey: n (udd) → p (uud): d → u + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ.

items.stem: Which interaction is responsible for β decay?
items.answer: the weak interaction
items.markingKey: Quark flavour changes only occur via the weak interaction.

items.stem: Use the quark model to describe β⁻ decay of a neutron.
items.answer: A neutron (udd) becomes a proton (uud): one down quark changes to an up quark, emitting an electron and an electron antineutrino via the weak interaction.
items.markingKey: udd → uud [1]; d → u [1]; e⁻ and ν̄ₑ emitted [1] [3]

items.stem: Which equation correctly shows the quark change in β⁺ decay?
items.answer: u → d + e⁺ + νₑ
items.markingKey: u → d + e⁺ + νₑ: charge +⅔ = −⅓ + 1 + 0; lepton number conserved.

items.stem: A nucleus of ¹⁴₆C undergoes β⁻ decay. (a) Write the nuclear equation. (b) State one property of the antineutrino.
items.answer: (a) ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e + ν̄ₑ (b) neutral / very small mass / rarely interacts
items.markingKey: (a) daughter [1]; e⁻ and ν̄ₑ [1] [2] (b) neutral / very small mass / rarely interacts [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which interaction is responsible for β decay? (b) Which particles are emitted with the up quark when a down quark changes in β⁻ decay?
items.answer: (a) the weak interaction (b) An electron and an electron antineutrino
items.markingKey: (a) Quark flavour changes only occur via the weak interaction. (b) d → u + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ.

items.stem: Use the quark model to describe β⁺ decay of a proton in a nucleus.
items.answer: A proton (uud) becomes a neutron (udd): one up quark changes to a down quark, emitting a positron and an electron neutrino.
items.markingKey: uud → udd [1]; u → d [1]; e⁺ and νₑ emitted [1] [3]

items.stem: Show that charge is conserved in the quark change u → d + e⁺ + νₑ.
items.answer: Left: +⅔e. Right: −⅓e + (+e) + 0 = +⅔e.
items.markingKey: left charge [1]; right charge sums to +⅔e [1] [2]

items.stem: Which equation correctly shows the quark change in β⁺ decay?
items.answer: u → d + e⁺ + νₑ

items.stem: For β⁻ decay, write the quark-level equation and show that charge is conserved. State the interaction responsible. Explain why an antineutrino, not a neutrino, is emitted.
items.answer: d → u + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ; charge: −⅓e = +⅔e − e + 0; weak interaction. Lepton number: the electron (+1) must be balanced by an antilepton (−1).
items.markingKey: equation [1]; charge balance [1]; weak interaction [1] ; lepton number argument [1] [4]

items.stem: A nucleus of ³₁H undergoes β⁻ decay. (a) Write the nuclear equation. (b) Show that charge is conserved in the quark change.
items.answer: (a) ³₁H → ³₂He + ⁰₋₁e + ν̄ₑ (b) −⅓e = +⅔e + (−e) + 0
items.markingKey: (a) daughter [1]; e⁻ and ν̄ₑ [1] [2] (b) −⅓e = +⅔e + (−e) + 0 [1]

items.stem: The radioactive isotope ⁶⁰₂₇Co decays by β⁻ emission. It is used as a tracer by researchers in Singapore. (a) Write the nuclear equation. (b) Show that charge is conserved in the quark change. (c) Name the interaction responsible.
items.answer: (a) ⁶⁰₂₇Co → ⁶⁰₂₈Ni + ⁰₋₁e + ν̄ₑ (b) −⅓e = +⅔e + (−e) + 0 (c) weak interaction

items.stem: A nucleus of ¹¹₆C (nucleon number 11, proton number 6) undergoes β⁺ decay. What are the nucleon number and proton number of the daughter nucleus?
items.answer: nucleon number 11, proton number 5
items.markingKey: ¹¹₆C → ¹¹₅B + ⁰₊₁e + νₑ; nucleon and proton numbers balance.

items.stem: A nucleus of ¹⁴₆C (nucleon number 14, proton number 6) undergoes β⁻ decay. What are the nucleon number and proton number of the daughter nucleus?
items.answer: nucleon number 14, proton number 7
items.markingKey: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e + ν̄ₑ; nucleon and proton numbers balance.

items.stem: A nucleus of ¹⁸₉F is a β⁺ emitter used in a research laboratory. (a) State what is meant by isotopes, using this element as an example. (b) State the antiparticle of the positron and how it differs. (c) Explain why the positrons emitted have a range of kinetic energies.
items.answer: (a) Nuclei with the same proton number (9) but different nucleon numbers. (b) The electron: same mass, opposite charge. (c) The energy released is shared with the neutrino in varying proportions.
items.markingKey: (a) Nuclei with the same proton number (9) but different nucleon numbers [1] (b) electron [1]; same mass opposite charge [1] [2] (c) The energy released is shared with the neutrino in varying proportions [1]

items.stem: A Σ⁺ baryon has quark composition uus. Calculate its charge and state whether it is a baryon, an antibaryon or a meson.
items.answer: +e; baryon

items.stem: Classify the proton as a hadron or a lepton and justify your answer by describing its structure. State whether it experiences the strong interaction.
items.answer: Hadron (baryon): made of three quarks uud; feels the strong force.
items.markingKey: correct class [1]; structure [1]; strong force statement [1] [3]

items.stem: The Λ⁰ baryon has quark composition uds. State the quark composition and the charge of its antiparticle, and explain how the masses compare.
items.answer: ūd̄s̄; charge 0; same mass as the Λ⁰ baryon
items.markingKey: each quark replaced by its antiquark (and vice versa): ūd̄s̄ [1]; charge 0 [1]; same mass [1] [3]

items.stem: A nucleus of ⁶⁰₂₇Co (nucleon number 60, proton number 27) undergoes β⁻ decay. Write the nuclear equation, showing nucleon and proton numbers, and state the particles emitted.
items.answer: ⁶⁰₂₇Co → ⁶⁰₂₈Ni + ⁰₋₁e + ν̄ₑ
items.markingKey: daughter nuclide correct [1]; emitted particle(s) with nucleon and proton numbers [1]; (anti)neutrino included [1] [3]

items.stem: A student at a summer school in Lagos is learning about the standard model of particle physics. (a) Use the quark model to show that the neutron is neutral. (b) The π⁻ meson has quark composition ūd. Determine its charge. (c) Name two leptons.
items.answer: (a) +⅔ − ⅓ − ⅓ = 0 (b) −⅔ − ⅓ = −e (c) electron and electron neutrino (also muon, tau, their neutrinos)
items.markingKey: (a) udd [1]; sum zero [1] [2] (b) −⅔ − ⅓ = −e [1] (c) electron and electron neutrino (also muon, tau, their neutrinos) [1]

items.stem: Explain why a free proton does not undergo β⁺ decay, although a proton in some nuclei can.
items.answer: A free neutron is more massive than a proton, so p → n + e⁺ + ν needs an energy input; inside a nucleus the change in nuclear binding energy can supply it.
items.markingKey: neutron heavier, energy needed [1]; nucleus provides energy [1] [2]

items.stem: A nucleus of ²²₁₁Na decays to ²²₁₀Ne. Identify the type of decay and describe the change at quark level, naming all the particles emitted.
items.answer: β⁺ decay: a proton (uud) becomes a neutron (udd); u → d + e⁺ + νₑ.
items.markingKey: type identified from change in Z [1]; quark change [1]; particles emitted [1] [3]

items.stem: Which equation correctly shows the quark change in β⁺ decay?
items.answer: u → d + e⁺ + νₑ
items.markingKey: u → d + e⁺ + νₑ: charge +⅔ = −⅓ + 1 + 0; lepton number conserved.

items.stem: The radioactive isotope ¹³⁷₅₅Cs decays by β⁻ emission. It is used as a tracer by researchers in Auckland. (a) Show that charge is conserved in the quark change. (b) Name the interaction responsible. (c) State one property of the antineutrino. (d) Compare this with the quark change in β⁺ decay.
items.answer: (a) −⅓e = +⅔e + (−e) + 0 (b) weak interaction (c) neutral / very small mass / rarely interacts (d) β⁺: up quark → down quark, emitting e⁺ and νₑ.
items.markingKey: (a) −⅓e = +⅔e + (−e) + 0 [1] (b) weak interaction [1] (c) neutral / very small mass / rarely interacts [1] (d) u → d [1]; positron and neutrino [1] [2]

items.stem: Why was a very thin gold foil used in the scattering experiment?
options: So that each α-particle was scattered by at most one nucleus
So that gold atoms could be seen
Because gold is a poor conductor
items.answer: So that each α-particle was scattered by at most one nucleus
items.markingKey: Thin foil avoids multiple scattering and absorption.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Describe the nuclear model of the atom. (b) Describe the observations of the α-particle scattering experiment and state the conclusion drawn from each.
items.answer: (a) A tiny, positively charged nucleus containing protons and neutrons (most of the mass) surrounded by negatively charged electrons at relatively large distances; mostly empty space. (b) Most passed straight through: atom mostly empty space. Some deflected through small angles: a positive charge concentrated in the atom. A very few deflected through > 90°: a tiny, dense, positive nucleus containing most of the mass.
items.markingKey: (a) small positive nucleus with most mass [1]; electrons outside, mostly empty space [1] [2] (b) most undeflected → empty space [1]; small deflections → positive charge [1]; large deflections → small massive nucleus [1] [3]

items.stem: An α-particle in a scattering experiment passes far from any nucleus. Describe and explain its path. Suggest how the path would differ for a higher-energy α-particle on the same initial line.
items.answer: It travels straight through with negligible deflection because the repulsive force is negligible at large distances. A higher-energy α-particle would be deflected less.
items.markingKey: path described [1]; explained by electrostatic repulsion [1]; effect of energy [1] [3]

items.stem: An atom of uranium has a diameter of about 3.5 × 10⁻¹⁰ m and its nucleus has a diameter of about 1.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. Work out the ratio of atomic diameter to nuclear diameter.
items.markingKey: 3.5 × 10⁻¹⁰/1.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ = 2.3 × 10⁴. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: An atom of uranium has a diameter of about 3.5 × 10⁻¹⁰ m and its nucleus about 1.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. In a scale model the nucleus is a marble 2.0 cm across. Calculate the diameter of the model atom in metres and use it to explain why most α-particles pass straight through a thin foil.
items.answer: 467 m; the nucleus occupies a tiny fraction of the atom so most α-particles do not pass near one.
items.markingKey: ratio = 2.3 × 10⁴ [1]; model diameter = 467 m [1]; mostly empty space explanation [1] [3]

items.stem: In 1909 Geiger and Marsden fired α-particles at a thin gold foil in a vacuum and counted scattered particles at different angles. A student in Karachi is studying their results. (a) State the observation that shows the atom is mostly empty space. (b) State the observation that shows that the nucleus contains most of the mass and is very small. (c) Explain why the experiment is carried out in a vacuum. (d) Explain why the foil must be very thin. (e) Sketch the paths of three α-particles passing at different distances from a nucleus.
items.answer: (a) Most α-particles passed straight through undeflected. (b) A very small number were deflected through angles greater than 90°. (c) α-particles would be absorbed/scattered by air molecules. (d) So each α-particle is scattered by only one nucleus. (e) distant: almost straight; nearer: small deflection; head-on: reflected back
items.markingKey: (a) Most α-particles passed straight through undeflected [1] (b) A very small number were deflected through angles greater than 90° [1] (c) α-particles would be absorbed/scattered by air molecules [1] (d) So each α-particle is scattered by only one nucleus [1] (e) distant path almost undeviated [1]; closer paths deflected more, head-on reflected back [1] [2]

items.stem: In β⁺ decay, which particles are emitted?
options: A positron and an electron antineutrino
An electron and an electron antineutrino
A positron and an electron neutrino
items.answer: A positron and an electron neutrino
items.markingKey: p → n + e⁺ + νₑ.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why γ-emission does not change the nucleon number or proton number of a nucleus. (b) Compare the charge, mass and penetrating power of α, β⁻ and γ radiation.
items.answer: (a) A γ-ray photon has no charge and no mass; it carries away only energy from an excited nucleus. (b) α: +2e, 4u, stopped by paper; β⁻: −e, ~1/2000 u, stopped by a few mm of aluminium; γ: no charge or mass, reduced by thick lead.
items.markingKey: (a) no charge and no mass [1]; only energy lost [1] [2] (b) charges [1]; masses [1]; penetration [1] [3]

items.stem: A nucleus of ¹³⁷₅₅Cs (nucleon number 137, proton number 55) undergoes β⁻ decay. What are the nucleon number and proton number of the daughter nucleus?
items.answer: nucleon number 137, proton number 56
items.markingKey: ¹³⁷₅₅Cs → ¹³⁷₅₆Ba + ⁰₋₁e + ν̄ₑ; nucleon and proton numbers balance.

items.stem: A nucleus of ¹³¹₅₃I (nucleon number 131, proton number 53) undergoes β⁻ decay. What are the nucleon number and proton number of the daughter nucleus?
items.answer: nucleon number 131, proton number 54
items.markingKey: ¹³¹₅₃I → ¹³¹₅₄Xe + ⁰₋₁e + ν̄ₑ; nucleon and proton numbers balance.

items.stem: A nucleus of ¹¹₆C is a β⁺ emitter used in a research laboratory. (a) State the numbers of protons and neutrons in the nucleus. (b) State what is meant by isotopes, using this element as an example. (c) State the antiparticle of the positron and how it differs.
items.answer: (a) 6 protons, 5 neutrons (b) Nuclei with the same proton number (6) but different nucleon numbers. (c) The electron: same mass, opposite charge.
items.markingKey: (a) both: 6 protons, 5 neutrons [1] (b) Nuclei with the same proton number (6) but different nucleon numbers [1] (c) electron [1]; same mass opposite charge [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which statement about an antiparticle is correct? (b) What is the quark composition of a proton?
items.answer: (a) It has the same mass as its particle but opposite charge (b) uud
items.markingKey: (a) Antiparticles have equal mass and opposite charge (and other quantum numbers). (b) Charge: +⅔ + ⅔ − ⅓ = +1.

items.stem: Classify the muon as a hadron or a lepton and justify your answer by describing its structure. State whether it experiences the strong interaction.
items.answer: Lepton: fundamental; does not feel the strong force.
items.markingKey: correct class [1]; structure [1]; strong force statement [1] [3]

items.stem: Which equation correctly shows the quark change in β⁻ decay?
items.answer: d → u + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ
items.markingKey: d → u + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ: charge −⅓ = +⅔ − 1 + 0; lepton number conserved.

items.stem: For β⁻ decay, write the quark-level equation and show that charge is conserved. State the interaction responsible.
items.answer: d → u + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ; charge: −⅓e = +⅔e − e + 0; weak interaction.
items.markingKey: equation [1]; charge balance [1]; weak interaction [1] [3]

items.stem: Particle accelerators produce many hadrons, which can be described by the quark model. (a) Use the quark model to show that the neutron is neutral. (b) The π⁻ meson has quark composition ūd. Determine its charge. (c) State what is meant by an antiparticle.
items.answer: (a) +⅔ − ⅓ − ⅓ = 0 (b) −⅔ − ⅓ = −e (c) A particle with the same mass but opposite charge (and other quantum numbers).
items.markingKey: (a) udd [1]; sum zero [1] [2] (b) −⅔ − ⅓ = −e [1] (c) A particle with the same mass but opposite charge (and other quantum numbers) [1]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why a free proton does not undergo β⁺ decay, although a proton in some nuclei can. (b) Use the quark model to describe β⁺ decay of a proton in a nucleus.
items.answer: (a) A free neutron is more massive than a proton, so p → n + e⁺ + ν needs an energy input; inside a nucleus the change in nuclear binding energy can supply it. (b) A proton (uud) becomes a neutron (udd): one up quark changes to a down quark, emitting a positron and an electron neutrino.
items.markingKey: (a) neutron heavier, energy needed [1]; nucleus provides energy [1] [2] (b) uud → udd [1]; u → d [1]; e⁺ and νₑ emitted [1] [3]

items.stem: A nucleus of ³₁H decays to ³₂He. Identify the type of decay and describe the change at quark level, naming all the particles emitted.
items.answer: β⁻ decay: a neutron (udd) becomes a proton (uud); d → u + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ.
items.markingKey: type identified from change in Z [1]; quark change [1]; particles emitted [1] [3]

items.stem: Which equation correctly shows the quark change in β⁻ decay?
items.answer: d → u + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ
items.markingKey: d → u + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ: charge −⅓ = +⅔ − 1 + 0; lepton number conserved.

(b) Name the interaction responsible. (c) State one property of the antineutrino. (d) Compare this with the quark change in β⁺ decay.
